I can’t edit the photo for you here because no image-editing/inspection tools are available in this session. I can’t access or modify the image directly. I can, however, give clear step‑by‑step instructions you can follow (or pass to someone who will edit the file) to remove the mug while keeping everything else unchanged. Tell me which editor you have (Photoshop, GIMP, Photopea, or command‑line/Python) and I’ll tailor steps. Meanwhile, here are effective options for each:

General preparatory tips (applies to all methods)
- Work non‑destructively: duplicate the background layer first and do edits on the copy.
- Zoom in to 100–200% for precise work; zoom out frequently to check global appearance.
- Select a slightly larger area than the mug (including a bit of surrounding background) for removal so blending looks natural.
- Preserve any product edges/reflections — use smaller brushes and careful masking near the product.
- If the mug casts a shadow you want to keep/replicate, plan to reconstruct or clone the shadow after removing the mug.

Photoshop (best for seamless results)
1. Duplicate the Background layer (Ctrl/Cmd+J).
2. Use Lasso or the Object Selection tool to select the mug plus a 5–20 px margin.
3. Edit > Content‑Aware Fill:
   - In the Content‑Aware Fill workspace, on the left preview, paint the green sampling area (exclude the product) so Photoshop uses appropriate source regions.
   - Settings: Color Adaptation = On, Rotation Adaptation = Auto, Scale = Auto. Output to Current Layer.
   - Apply and inspect.
4. Use the Spot Healing Brush (Content‑Aware) or Healing Brush to refine small texture mismatches.
   - For Healing Brush sample from nearby clean background (Alt/Option-click).
   - Use low hardness (0–30%), size a bit larger than the defect.
5. If any structural area (e.g., wood grain or product edge) needs repair, use the Clone Stamp tool on a new layer (Sample: Current & Below), set opacity 70–100% and clone carefully from matching areas.
6. Recreate/adjust shadow if needed:
   - Add a new layer set to Multiply, sample a mid‑gray/black from existing shadow, paint with a soft brush at low opacity (10–30%), then Gaussian Blur and transform to match the original shadow direction and softness.
7. Flatten or export when satisfied.

Photopea (web, Photoshop‑like)
- Photopea supports similar tools (Spot Healing, Clone Stamp, Patch). Follow the same steps as Photoshop using Photopea’s Content‑Aware Fill (Edit > Content-Aware Fill) or Patch tool + Healing Brush. Work on duplicated layer.

GIMP (free; best with Resynthesizer plugin)
1. Duplicate the layer.
2. Select the mug with Free Select or Rectangle Select with feathering ~5–20 px.
3. If you have the Resynthesizer plugin:
   - Filters > Enhance > Heal Selection. Use default settings and tweak radius (e.g., 15–50 px) until result looks natural.
4. If no plugin:
   - Use Clone Tool (C) and Healing Tool (H). Sample nearby background regions frequently (Ctrl+click), clone carefully, and use Healing to blend.
5. Rebuild shadows on an upper layer set to Multiply with a soft low‑opacity brush, then blur and transform.

Command‑line / Python (OpenCV) — quick automated approach (works well for simple backgrounds)
- This is suitable if the background is mostly uniform or repetitive texture. It can require some manual cleanup afterward.

Example Python using OpenCV inpainting:
1. Create a mask image (same size) where the mug area is white (255) and everything else black (0). You can draw the mask in any editor.
2. Run:

import cv2
img = cv2.imread('photo.jpg')
mask = cv2.imread('mask.png', 0)  # white area = region to inpaint
# Try Telea method first
res_telea = cv2.inpaint(img, mask, 3, cv2.INPAINT_TELEA)
cv2.imwrite('inpaint_telea.jpg', res_telea)
# Also try Navier-Stokes
res_ns = cv2.inpaint(img, mask, 3, cv2.INPAINT_NS)
cv2.imwrite('inpaint_ns.jpg', res_ns)

- Radius (3) may need adjustment (3–10) depending on image resolution. Inspect both outputs; pick the better and refine with manual cloning/healing in an image editor.

Tips for preserving product edges and reflections
- Make a tighter manual selection close to the product boundary and exclude the product pixels from automated fills (so the algorithm doesn’t smear the product).
- Use layer masks and paint in cloned patches gradually rather than one big automatic pass when near the product.
- For reflective surfaces: clone small patches of similar reflection areas and blend with low opacity. Work in small steps.

If you want, I can:

- Provide a step‑by‑step Video/YouTube tutorial links (if you tell me you want them; I’ll cite links if you ask).
- Walk you through the edit interactively if you tell me which tool you’re using.
